old: either by fortune or by virtù — a man's own skill and nerve.
new: either by fortune or by virtù.
why: Italian ends on the bare pair 'o per fortuna o per virtù' (Marriott: 'by fortune or by ability'); the definition is the editor's and belongs in the glossary, not the sentence. Editor: add a 'virtù' glossary entry to enrichment and update the Chapter I divergence note ('glossed once at this first use').

old: my lady of Forli,
new: my lady of Forlì,
why: Spelling standardized to 'Forlì' as in XX (Italian Furlì/Forlì); work-wide name consistency.

old: being all slaves, and bound men, are corrupted
new: being all slaves and beholden to him, are corrupted
why: Italian 'sendo tutti stiavi e obligati' is one phrase: slaves and bound by obligation to the lord. 'Bondmen' (report's fix) would misread obligati as serfdom; 'beholden to him' is both truer and smoother.

old: the repeated rebellions of Spain, of France, and of Greece against the Romans
new: the repeated rebellions of Spain, of Gaul, and of Greece against the Romans
why: Italian 'Francia' here is Roman Gaul; 'France' sets the kingdom of the previous paragraph rebelling against Rome.

old: the moment the crowd began not to believe him
new: the moment the crowd stopped believing him
why: Italian 'cominciò a non crederli'; the literal 'began not to believe' trips aloud. Same sense.

old: from there he earned his promotion to prince
new: from there he earned the right to be made their prince
why: Italian 'da quivi meritò d'essere fatto loro principe'; 'promotion' has an office ring and drops 'their'.

old: and partly insured against present dangers
new: and partly secured against present dangers
why: Italian 'in parte assicurato de' presenti periculi'; 'insured' now reads as a policy.

old: he pounced on Pisa. After that, Lucca and Siena would fold at once
new: he would have pounced on Pisa. After that, Lucca and Siena would have folded at once
why: Italian imperfects 'saltava in Pisa ... Lucca e Siena cedeva subito' are counterfactual, the plan cut off by Alexander's death (Borgia never took Pisa); 'pounced' reports it as done, then the sentence slides into 'would'.

old: he lived a criminal life at every stage of his career
new: he lived a criminal life at every age
why: Italian 'per li gradi della sua età', the stages of his life, not his career; 'career' also anticipates the soldiering that follows.

old: after entering the militia, he rose through its ranks
new: after joining the army, he rose through its ranks
why: Italian 'voltosi alla milizia' is the military life; a modern 'militia' is a citizen reserve or irregular band, wrong for Agathocles.

old: up through the ranks of the militia
new: up through the ranks of the army
why: Same 'milizia' as seg-0002 ('per li gradi della milizia'); keep the two consistent.

old: but converted into the greatest usefulness to the subjects that they can be.
new: but turned, as far as possible, to the subjects' benefit.
why: Italian 'si convertiscono in più utilità de' sudditi che si può'; the trailing 'that they can be' buries the point. Same sense.

old: out of faint-heartedness — a natural shortage of spine — then
new: out of faint-heartedness and a natural lack of courage, then
why: Italian is a plain pair, 'pusillanimità e defetto naturale d'animo'; the dash makes the second half read as an editor's gloss, and 'shortage of spine' is colloquial.

old: he ruins you in the ordinary way — by losing.
new: he ruins you in the ordinary way.
why: Italian 'ti rovina per l'ordinario' stops there; 'by losing' explains the joke into the text.

old: as happened later at Vaila,
new: as happened later at Vailà,
why: Machiavelli's 'Vailà'; standardized with XX.

old: took Imola and Forli.
new: took Imola and Forlì.
why: Spelling standardized to 'Forlì' as in XX.

old: he should live in the hunt, hardening
new: he should always be out hunting, hardening
why: Italian 'debbe stare sempre in sulle caccie'; 'live in the hunt' is a calque, and it also drops 'sempre'.

old: another a miser — I use the Tuscan word, since in our tongue an avaricious man is still one who craves to get by plunder, while we call a miser the man who holds back too hard from using what is his own; one is a giver
new: another a miser (I use the Tuscan word, since in our tongue an avaricious man is still one who craves to get by plunder, while we call a miser the man who holds back too hard from using what is his own); one is a giver
why: The Italian sets 'usando uno termine toscano ...' in parentheses; the dash here never closes, so the list resumes inside the aside.

old: he may let those go with less concern
new: he may indulge in them with less concern
why: Italian 'vi si può con meno respetto lasciare andare' = he may give himself over to those lesser vices; 'let those go' reads as giving them up, the opposite.

old: Res dura, et regni novitas me talia cogunt moliri, et late fines custode tueri.
new:
Res dura, et regni novitas me talia cogunt
moliri, et late fines custode tueri.
why: Aeneid I.563-64, two hexameters, break after 'cogunt'; verse keeps its line (newline is how other Lectio editions carry verse). Note: the build currently collapses newlines in this prose-form work (XXVI's Petrarch is already lined in pipeline/modern but prints as one line), so this shows only once that is fixed.

old: men being wretched, is broken
new: men being wicked, is broken
why: Italian 'per essere gli uomini tristi': tristi is wicked/base; 'wretched' now first means miserable and turns contempt into pity.

old: taught to princes under cover by the ancient writers
new: taught to princes in veiled form by the ancient writers
why: Italian 'copertamente', figuratively; 'under cover' now suggests spying.

old: because they are wretched, and would not keep
new: because they are wicked, and would not keep
why: Italian 'perché sono tristi'; same word and fix as XVII.

old: the Parlement — the high court — and its authority
new: the Parlement and its authority
why: Italian 'el parlamento e l'autorità sua'; the gloss is the editor's. Editor: gloss 'Parlement' in enrichment.

old: Julianus the emperor being known for his slackness, Severus persuaded
new: Knowing how slack the emperor Julianus was, Severus persuaded
why: Italian 'Conosciuto Severo la ignavia di Iuliano imperatore': Severus is the one who knows; the absolute construction is stiff and hides that. ('Sluggard' in the report is archaic.)

old: He then went to find him in France,
new: He then went to find him in Gaul,
why: Italian 'in Francia' is Roman Gaul (Albinus, AD 197); consistent with IV.

old: mercenary soldiery, which is what was said of it above;
new: mercenary soldiery, which is of the kind described above;
why: Italian 'la quale è di quella qualità che di sopra è detto'; the current clause attaches to nothing.

old: Such methods, besides, argue weakness in the prince
new: Such methods, besides, betray weakness in the prince
why: Italian 'Arguiscono ... debolezza'; 'argue' for 'indicate' is a calque few readers still carry.

old: newly taken a state by means of inside support from within it
new: newly taken a state with help from inside it
why: Italian 'mediante e' favori intrinsechi di quello'; 'inside ... from within' doubles.

old: and you will have no defense to offer and no reason anyone should give you one, and no one will take you in.
new: and you will have no claim and nothing else to defend you or take you in.
why: Italian 'non arai ragione né cosa alcuna che ti defenda né che ti riceva': one phrase, no claim and nothing to defend or shelter you; the three 'and' clauses also shift the sense.

old: a lover of excellence, giving a place to able men
new: a lover of virtù, giving a place to able men
why: Virtù policy: Italian 'amatore delle virtù, dando recapito alli uomini virtuosi'. Noun kept as virtù; the adjective stays English ('able').

old: for fear of the taxman.
new: for fear of taxes.
why: Italian 'per paura delle taglie', levies; 'the taxman' is breezy. ('Open a business' for 'aprire uno traffico' is fine and kept.)

old: on you yourself and on your own strength.
new: on you yourself and on your own virtù.
why: Virtù policy: Italian 'che dependino da te proprio e dalla virtù tua'. This closing line sets up XXV's virtù-against-fortune; missed by the report.

old: where no ordered strength stands ready to resist her
new: where no ordered virtù stands ready to resist her
why: Italian 'dove non è ordinata virtù a resisterle'; the chapter that pits virtù against fortune must not drop the word.

old: protected by proper strength,
new: protected by proper virtù,
why: Italian 'riparata da conveniente virtù'; same policy.

old: for the power in Moses to show itself
new: for the virtù of Moses to show itself
why: Italian 'a volere conoscere la virtù di Moisè'; callback to VI, which uses virtù for Moses.

old: for the worth of one Italian spirit to be known
new: for the virtù of one Italian spirit to be known
why: Italian 'volendo conoscere la virtù d'uno spirito italiano'.

old: with its fortune and its ability,
new: with its fortune and its virtù,
why: Italian 'con la fortuna e virtù sua'.

old: as if military virtue were spent
new: as if military virtù were spent
why: Italian 'sia spenta la virtù militare'; same policy (low: 'military virtue' already near).

old: Here there is great strength in the limbs
new: Here there is great virtù in the limbs
why: Italian 'Qui è virtù grande nelle membra'. ('Superior in strength' below is 'con le forze' and stays.)

old: by ability or by fortune,
new: by virtù or by fortune,
why: Italian 'e per virtù e per fortuna'.

old: then Allesandria, Capua, Genoa, Vaila, Bologna, Mestri.
new: then Alessandria, Capua, Genoa, Vailà, Bologna, Mestri.
why: 'Allesandria' is a misprint carried from Marriott's text (his own note spells Alessandria); 'Vailà' standardized with XII and XX.

old: with Italian strength we can defend ourselves
new: with Italian virtù we can defend ourselves
why: Italian 'per potere con la virtù italica defendersi'; missed by the report, same policy.
